topics.title: Knife skills in eight cards
topics.dek: The grip, the claw, the three cuts and why a dull knife is the dangerous one

slides.h: One good knife does almost everything
slides.p: An 8-inch chef's knife handles ninety percent of kitchen work. Add a small paring knife for peeling and a serrated bread knife for crusts and tomatoes, and you're equipped. Price matters less than keeping it sharp.

slides.h: Pinch the blade, don't hold the handle
slides.p: Pinch the blade just ahead of the handle between thumb and the side of your bent index finger, with the other three fingers around the handle. It feels odd for a day and then gives you control the handle grip never will.

items: Thumb on one side of the blade's heel
Bent index finger on the other
Wrist loose, elbow does the lifting

slides.h: The other hand makes a claw
slides.p: Curl the fingertips of your guiding hand under so the knuckles face the blade. The flat of the blade rides against the knuckles; the fingertips are tucked out of reach. Move the claw back a little for each slice and the knife follows.

items: Blade's flat side touches the knuckles
Thumb and pinky hold the food from behind
Fingers flat on the board, pointing at the blade

slides.h: Rock, don't chop
slides.p: Keep the tip on the board and rock the blade down and forward through the food in one motion, then lift the heel and bring it back. Slicing forward does the cutting; pushing straight down crushes. Let the weight of the knife work.

slides.h: Three cuts cover most recipes
slides.p: A dice is cubes: small (¼ in), medium (½ in), large (¾ in). Julienne is matchsticks, about 2 inches by ⅛ inch. Chiffonade is leafy herbs stacked, rolled and sliced into ribbons. Even sizes matter more than tiny sizes: even pieces cook at the same rate.

slides.h: Make a flat side first
slides.p: A round thing rolls; a rolling thing cuts you. Halve the onion, trim a slice off the carrot, cut the squash in two so it sits flat. Then everything you do is on a stable base. The same goes for the board: a damp towel underneath stops it skating.

slides.h: A dull knife is the dangerous one
slides.p: A dull edge needs force and slips off the skin of a tomato instead of biting. Hone before each use (the steel realigns the edge; it doesn't sharpen) and sharpen when honing stops helping, every few months with a whetstone or a decent pull-through sharpener.

slides.h: Boards, washing and the one rule
slides.p: Wood or plastic are both fine if they're cleaned; a separate board for raw meat is the real safeguard. Wash knives by hand right away and put them back; a knife in a sink of suds is a trap. Never try to catch a falling knife. Step back, let it land.

items: Hand wash, dry, put away at once
Carry it point down, blade back
Dishwasher: dulls the edge, loosens handles

quiz.q: The safest way to hold the food you're cutting is…
a: Fingers flat, pointing at the blade
A claw, fingertips tucked, knuckles against the blade
quiz.why: The knuckles become a guide for the flat of the blade and the fingertips are out of its path.

quiz.q: Running a knife along a honing steel…
quiz.why: Honing straightens the microscopic edge that folds over in use. Sharpening on a stone removes metal to create a new edge.

quiz.q: A knife slips from your hand toward the floor. You should…
a: Step back and let it fall
quiz.why: Hands and feet out of the way. A knife can be picked up; a cut tendon can't be undone.

take: Pinch grip on the blade, claw on the food, rock the tip on the board.
Hone every time, sharpen every few months; the dull knife is the one that cuts you.

topics.title: How to read a nutrition label
topics.dek: The serving-size trap, the 5/20 rule and the one line that changed

slides.h: Start at the top: the serving
slides.p: Every number on the label is per serving, and the serving is what people typically eat, not what they should. A 20-ounce bottle may be 2.5 servings. Multiply by what you actually ate before anything else makes sense.

v.c: a 20 oz soda is often 2.5 servings; multiply everything

slides.h: Calories are big for a reason
slides.p: The redesigned U.S. label puts calories in large bold type. Two thousand a day is the reference used for the percentages; most people need somewhere between 1,600 and 3,000 depending on size, age and activity.

v.c: where a day's calories commonly come from

slides.h: The 5/20 rule
slides.p: Percent Daily Value (%DV) is on the right. Five percent or less is low; twenty percent or more is high. Aim low for saturated fat, sodium and added sugars; aim high for fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron and potassium.

slides.h: Added sugars finally have their own line
slides.p: Since 2020, labels separate the sugar that occurs naturally (in milk, fruit) from sugar that was added. The daily value for added sugar is 50 grams; a can of soda can use most of it. Four grams is roughly a teaspoon.

slides.h: Sodium hides in bread, not just chips
slides.p: The limit most guidelines use is 2,300 milligrams a day, about a teaspoon of salt. More than seventy percent of it comes from packaged and restaurant food: bread, deli meat, soup, sauces, cheese. Look at the mg, not just the taste.

slides.h: Fats: which kind matters more than how much
slides.p: Saturated fat (meat, butter, coconut) is listed with a daily value of 20 grams; trans fat should be zero. Unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fish) aren't limited and aren't always listed. Low-fat often means more sugar; read the whole panel.

slides.h: Fiber and protein: the lines to want more of
slides.p: The fiber daily value is 28 grams and most people get about half. Whole grains, beans, fruit and vegetables carry it. Protein has no %DV unless a claim is made; 15 to 20 grams per meal is a common target.

slides.h: The ingredient list is in order of weight
slides.p: The first ingredient is the biggest. If sugar (or any of its names: corn syrup, dextrose, cane juice, maltose) is in the top three, it's a sweet. Short lists you can picture are usually a good sign. 'Natural flavors' is a flavor you aren't told about.

quiz.q: A %DV of 25% for sodium on a label means the serving is…
quiz.why: Twenty percent or more is high; five percent or less is low. Sodium is one to aim low on.

quiz.q: Ingredients on a label are listed…
a: In the order they were added
quiz.why: The first ingredient is the largest share. Sugar near the top means a sugary product, whatever the front says.

a: Only sugar from fruit and milk
quiz.why: Natural sugar in milk or fruit is in 'Total Sugars'; the added line is what the maker put in. Daily value: 50 grams.

take: Serving size first; multiply by what you ate.
5% is low, 20% is high: low for saturated fat, sodium and added sugar, high for fiber.
Ingredients are listed by weight; sugar in the top three means dessert.
src: FDA: How to understand and use the Nutrition Facts label

topics.title: Coffee, from bean to cup
topics.dek: Two species, four roasts, one ratio and why your brew tastes sour or bitter

slides.h: Two beans run the world
slides.p: Arabica is about sixty percent of production: sweeter, more acidic, grown high and cool. Robusta is hardier, higher in caffeine (about twice as much), harsher, and the base of most instant coffee and many espresso blends for its crema and punch.

slides.h: A coffee 'bean' is a fruit seed
slides.p: The cherry is picked, the fruit removed (washed, or dried on the seed as a 'natural'), the green seeds dried, sorted and shipped. Everything you taste as 'coffee' comes later, in the roaster, in about ten to fifteen minutes.

slides.h: Roast is a dial from bright to burnt
slides.p: Light roasts stop soon after the beans first crack, keeping the origin's acidity and fruit. Medium balances sweetness and body. Dark goes past the second crack: oily, smoky, bitter, with the origin mostly gone. Darker roasts have slightly less caffeine by volume, not more.

slides.h: Grind to match the method
slides.p: The finer the grind, the faster water pulls flavor out. Espresso's 25-second shot needs powder; a French press steeping for four minutes needs coarse grounds that won't slip through the mesh. Buy whole beans and grind just before brewing; ground coffee goes stale in days.

slides.h: The golden ratio
slides.p: About one gram of coffee to sixteen grams of water, give or take: 60 grams per litre, or two level tablespoons per 6-ounce cup. A kitchen scale ends the guessing. Stronger coffee means more grounds, not a darker roast or a longer brew.

v.c: coffee to water by weight; about 60 g per litre

slides.h: Water: hot, but not boiling
slides.p: Brew between about 195 and 205 °F (90–96 °C). Boiling water scorches the grounds; water much cooler under-extracts. Off the boil for thirty seconds is right. Coffee is 98 percent water, so if your tap tastes bad, so will the cup; filtered is better than distilled.

slides.h: Sour means under, bitter means over
slides.p: Extraction pulls out acids first, then sugars, then bitter compounds. Sour, thin and salty means you stopped early: grind finer, brew longer, water hotter. Bitter, harsh and drying means you went too far: grind coarser, brew shorter. Adjust one thing at a time.

slides.h: Fresh beats fancy
slides.p: Roasted coffee peaks from a few days to about a month after the roast date; after that the aromatics fade. Buy small bags with a roast date, keep them sealed and dark at room temperature, and skip the fridge, where beans pick up moisture and smells.

quiz.q: Your coffee tastes sour and thin. The usual fix is to…
a: Grind finer and brew a little longer
quiz.why: Sour means under-extraction: the acids came out but the sugars didn't. More contact time or a finer grind pulls the sweetness through.

quiz.q: Which has more caffeine per bean?
quiz.why: Robusta carries roughly twice the caffeine of arabica, part of why it's harsher and more bitter.

quiz.q: A French press needs grounds that are…
quiz.why: Four minutes of steeping extracts slowly, and coarse grounds stay behind the mesh plunger.

take: 1:16 by weight, water just off the boil, grind matched to the method.
Sour is under-extracted, bitter is over; change one variable at a time.
Whole beans, roast date on the bag, used within a month.

topics.title: The temperatures that keep you safe
topics.dek: The danger zone, the thermometer numbers and the two-hour rule

slides.h: The danger zone: 40 to 140
slides.p: Between 40 °F and 140 °F (4–60 °C) bacteria can double every twenty minutes. Cold storage keeps food below it; cooking takes food above it; the time in between is what makes people sick. Nearly every rule on these cards is about that window.

slides.h: Two hours, or one when it's hot
slides.p: Perishable food (meat, dairy, cooked rice, cut fruit) that sits out more than two hours should be thrown away; one hour if the room or the picnic is above 90 °F. The clock includes the time on the counter before and after the meal.

v.c: out of the fridge; 1 hour above 90 °F

slides.h: A thermometer, not a color
slides.p: Juices and pink centers lie; burgers brown before they're safe and chicken can stay pink when done. Push an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part, away from bone, and read it. It is the single most useful cheap tool in the kitchen.

slides.h: Thaw in the fridge, not on the counter
slides.p: A frozen chicken left out thaws from the outside in; the surface spends hours in the danger zone while the middle is still ice. Thaw in the fridge (a day per 4–5 pounds), in cold water changed every 30 minutes, or in the microwave if you'll cook it right away.

items: Cold water, sealed bag, changed every 30 min
On the counter or in the sink overnight

slides.h: Don't wash the chicken
slides.p: Rinsing raw poultry spreads bacteria up to three feet around the sink in droplets; cooking kills them, water doesn't. Wash your hands for 20 seconds, the board, the knife and the counter instead. Produce, on the other hand, does get rinsed under running water.

slides.h: Cross-contamination is the quiet culprit
slides.p: Raw juices on a board, a knife or your hands move onto food that won't be cooked. Separate boards (or wash between), raw meat on the bottom fridge shelf, a clean plate for the cooked burgers, never the one they came out on.

items: Raw meat on its own board
Wash hands, board and knife before touching anything else
Cooked food onto a clean plate
Marinade that touched raw meat is not a sauce (boil it, or make fresh)

slides.h: Cool fast, reheat hot
slides.p: A deep pot of soup can sit in the danger zone for hours in the fridge. Split it into shallow containers, leave the lids loose until cold, and it's safe. Reheat leftovers to 165 °F, steaming throughout; stir microwaved food, which heats unevenly.

slides.h: Rice and the bacteria that survive cooking
slides.p: Bacillus cereus spores live through cooking and multiply in rice left warm. Serve it hot, cool it within an hour and refrigerate, and eat it within a day. The same goes for pasta and cooked grains. Reheated rice is fine; rice that sat out warm isn't.

quiz.why: Between 40 and 140 °F bacteria multiply fast. Keep cold food below it and hot food above it.

quiz.q: Chicken is safe to eat at an internal temperature of…
quiz.why: 165 °F in the thickest part, away from bone. Color and juices are not reliable.

quiz.q: The best way to thaw a frozen roast is…
a: In the fridge, a day per 4–5 pounds
quiz.why: The counter leaves the surface in the danger zone for hours. The fridge, cold water or the microwave keep it safe.

take: 40–140 °F is the danger zone; two hours is the limit outside the fridge.
Thermometer, not color: 165 poultry, 160 ground, 145 whole cuts and fish.
Don't wash the chicken; do wash your hands, the board and the knife.
src: CDC: Four steps to food safety
